request.system:
You choose the delivery workflow for a requirement in a governed software delivery pipeline. Each workflow is a fixed sequence of stages, gates and human checkpoints; choosing the wrong one means the work is governed for the wrong risks (for example, a bug fixed without first reproducing it, or an API change released without an API definition and documentation).

You are given the requirement as written, the workflows that are eligible (rules have already excluded the others, for example by whether a codebase exists), each with a description and when to use it, and facts about the workspace.

Choose the workflow whose `use_when` best matches what the requirement asks for. Judge by the substance of the request, not its wording or length: a report of something that should work but does not is a defect even if it never says "bug"; a request that changes what clients of the API can do, or asks for API definitions, documentation or release preparation, needs the full lifecycle.

Return:
- `workflow`: the chosen workflow's name.
- `confidence`: high when one workflow clearly fits; medium when another is plausible; low when the requirement is unclear about what kind of change it is. A person confirms every choice; low confidence tells them to look closely.
- `rationale`: two or three sentences a reviewer can check against the requirement.
- `signals`: short quotations or paraphrases from the requirement that drove the choice.
- `runner_up`: the next best workflow, or "none".

Never choose a workflow because it is shorter or cheaper. If a reviewer rejected an earlier proposal with a comment, follow the comment.

<requirement>
# Bug report: links to some valid websites cannot be shortened

> Input to the orchestrator's bug-fix workflow. The service in `url-shortener/` is in use.

## What users report
Support has received several reports from users who cannot shorten links to websites that open
fine in their browser. Creating the link fails immediately with:

    400 {"error":"invalid_url","message":"url must include a host"}

Examples from the tickets:
- `https://müller.de/angebote` (a German shop)
- `https://例え.jp/` (a Japanese site)
- `https://my_site.example.com/page` (an internal-looking but public host name with an underscore)

The same shop works when a user pastes its address as `https://xn--mller-kva.de/angebote`, which is
how some browsers display it when copied. Ordinary addresses such as `https://example.com/café`
work.

## Expected
Any link that a browser can open and that the service's destination rules allow can be shortened,
and its short link redirects to it. The error message should not claim that a URL with a host has
no host.

## Constraints
- The destination rules must not be weakened: links to local, private or otherwise prohibited
  addresses must still be refused, whatever form their host name is written in.
- Existing links and endpoints keep working unchanged.

## Known open points (for the Analyst to resolve or flag)
- Whether the short link should redirect to the address exactly as the user entered it, or to an
  equivalent normalized form.
</requirement>

data.rationale: This is a defect report: URLs users expect the service to accept are rejected with `invalid_url`, despite having a host and being browser-accessible. The expected behavior is to accept allowed destinations and redirect to them, so the workflow should reproduce the failure with a regression test before fixing it.
signals: “cannot shorten links to websites that open fine in their browser”
The service returns `400 ... "url must include a host"` for internationalized and underscore-containing hosts
“Any link that a browser can open and that the service's destination rules allow can be shortened”
